title: Zazen
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing both the ordinary and extraordinary aspects of reality in Zen practice. By cultivating a sense of acceptance, groundedness, and allowingness, we can develop a direct and accepting relationship with our lives, rather than trying to control or manipulate them. This ordinary quality of zazen allows us to approach difficult situations with a sense of fundamental okay-ness, freeing us from reactive patterns and enabling us to live more fully in the present moment.

It just means, za means sit, and zen is zen, so it's just sit zen.
We add interpretation to it so easily, like meditation or something.
Zazen is zazen.
If you look around, look at where people's bodies are, it does seem to be the main activity that we do at our meetings, this zazen.

That everything we do, all the ritual and all the walking practice and the chanting and everything, somehow has zazen behind it or zazen beneath it or penetrating through it.
And so I thought it would be nice to focus a little bit on zazen itself, if there is such a thing.

What came to me as a way to think about it, when I was thinking about it, was a pairing of two big areas or two major aspects, which for some reason tonight I want to call the ordinary and the extraordinary.
So I'm going to suggest tonight that zazen, as a way of speaking about it for now anyway, has a quality of ordinariness and a quality of extraordinariness.
And it's funny, the minute I wrote that, I pictured hearing that and imagined our conditioned minds find the ordinary kind of boring and, well, ordinary.
And the extraordinary, that sounds good, that's probably what spiritual practice will get me.
But I don't want to suggest that it's really that way, it's just a way that our minds quickly rank things.
Both of these dimensions are equally essential, equally important, ordinary and extraordinary.
With the big caveat through this whole little thing that these aren't really real categories anyway.
They actually collapse into each other.
It's a way of talking, but since words are all we've got, we need ways to talk about things that are hard to talk about.
So the ordinary dimension of zazen would be the wondrous quality of settling that zazen offers us.
You know how little by little, through the practice, we become more settled into our life.

It's not a straight-line thing, there's big dips and jags and eruptions and God knows what, but on the whole, over time, through zazen practice we are supported, and we support ourselves in being more settled into our life, more settled in our body, and more settled into the things that happen.
But difficult things are still difficult.
It's a mistake to think that we will somehow launch into some state of permanent bliss, everything is one.
That's not what we're after here.
Maybe there's a way to do that, or maybe that's a kind of mental illness, I don't know.
But the ordinary subtleness of zazen is not that everything is great, but it's also not that everything is terrible.
It's actually just: everything is.
And it's not that difficult things don't still bother us, but they don't bother us in the same way as we practice this ordinary zazen.
Difficult things are still difficult, but the difficulty, we experience it very differently.
It's hard to explain in a way, but it also makes perfect sense.
And it's a total game changer over time to have a life that's not so much run by preferences and desires and wanting things to always be nice.
And there's nothing wrong with nice and pleasant, there's nothing wrong with desire exactly either.

But when you are sick or in difficult circumstances or some horrible thing happens in the world, the subtleness is not that you don't mind, it's no big deal, but that you see the is-ness of it and the fundamental okay-ness of it, it is just as it is.
You don't fight it and you don't complain.
Because how could you complain?
How could it be any other way than it is?
One way to think about all this is that great metaphor from the Salata Sutta, early Buddhist Sutta we talked about a month ago maybe.
As we become more grounded in this ordinary dimension of zazen, we stop throwing second darts.
And if you haven't heard that teaching, that metaphor of Buddhas, the idea is that when we feel the pains of life, it's like being hit by a dart, and it does hurt.
Of course it does, pain is pain.
And it's just as counterproductive to not deeply acknowledge and feel the hurt, to experience what is.
So there's this first dart.
But then we have this powerful tendency to throw a second dart at ourselves.
And the second dart is usually some version of this shouldn't be happening.
Some combination of blame, denial, anger, aversion.
And of course that is actually conditioned, and it's not like we should feel bad if we do it, it's from our conditioned selves.
But as we settle in ordinary zazen, naturally we do this less and less, and ultimately it just doesn't even occur to us.
It's not like we need to memorize all these techniques and teachings and be hypervigilant every second, right?
Like, okay, need to remember, don't throw second darts, that really is bad, makes me suffer.
It's okay to practice that way.

But ultimately zazen supports us in another way of approaching these things: a direct seeing, feeling, and experiencing of our lives, where you don't have to catch yourself and clamp down and stop yourself from complaining.
The urge to complain just doesn't arise, like why would it arise?
You can see that things have happened just the way they happened.
And it's also not to say that the influence of your choices and the choices of our friends and colleagues and people all around the planet won't change it next time.
Of course they very well may, but what has happened has happened.
No point fighting it.

And I think you practice for a while, you also notice that you don't always even notice when this ordinary manifestation of zazen is helping you, and it's helping the people around you, probably helps them even more than you.

Because the result of this ordinary practice is an ordinary life, living day by day, moment by moment, responding to things, appreciating things, being with things, being also with the difficult things, but they come and go like everything else.

But sometimes you can look back and realize, oh wow, I could have been really reactive about that, I could have been really complaining, I could have been throwing darts left, right and center there, but I didn't.
Isn't that nice?
Helpful.
An example for me came up today.
One of my karmic conditioned quirks, I think, is that I'm a bit greedy and protective about my time and attention.
And I'm pretty busy, or at least I tell myself I'm pretty busy, and probably more or less true, objectively, if there's any such thing as objective.

And reality comes and knocks my hand, the plan goes falling away.
But then I see it fall, and I can usually let it go.
There's actually kind of a relief.
Sometimes I've noticed I have these plans for the day, all the things I need to get done, and something intercedes and I don't get to follow my plan.
And actually somehow I feel better, like it works out better.
Strange stuff.
That's something to do with the way we're always trying to predict what's going to happen, when we're always pretty much wrong.
